1.why: The reset token is generated and stored per-session, and verify-token compares the submitted token against that session's own session.resetToken via timingSafeEqual, binding the code to the requesting user/session.

2.why: A token validates only against the requesting session's stored resetToken, so the same code cannot work in any other session; the statement is false.

3.why: Password reset performs no invalidation of other sessions — sessions persist in the map until TTL expiry with their authenticated flags intact, so previous sessions remain usable.

4.why: TLS is mandatory (the process exits without certs, HTTP only 308-redirects to HTTPS, HSTS is set), but no explicit TLS version floor (e.g., TLS 1.3 only) is configured in the code.

5.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed and tokens are CSPRNG-generated with TLS in transit, but reset codes sit as plaintext in memory and nothing is encrypted at rest, so 'encrypted' holds only partially.

6.why: No email exists; the simulated in-browser delivery message is generic with no personal data, yet it openly displays the reset token in the page and log panel.

7.why: All inputs pass strict allowlist validators (account regex, token, MFA, password policy) and the client renders exclusively via textContent, never innerHTML.

8.why: The only redirect is a hardcoded 308 to https://localhost:3000/, API calls enforce a same-origin check, and no user-controlled redirect targets exist anywhere.

9.why: There are no email templates, and the single HTML page embeds no user input — the DOM is built with textContent and all scripts/styles are nonce-protected under CSP.

10.why: Error responses are generic, but the API returns testToken/testMfaCode and the UI 'Logs' panel displays the reset token and MFA code, so tokens are shown in logs.

11.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed and reset tokens are random in-memory values, but the MFA code is hardcoded as "482913" directly in the source code.

12.why: No default accounts or passwords exist and a strong password policy is enforced; only the static simulated MFA code resembles a default code.

13.why: failedAttempt tracks failures per action and, after MAX_FAILURES (5), sets a 60-second block returning a generic 429 response.

14.why: The recover endpoint returns the identical generic message for every request with no account lookup, so account existence is never disclosed.

15.why: Reset codes are 32-byte crypto.getRandomValues base64url values, single-use (resetUsed), 10-minute TTL, and stored only on the requesting session.
